title: The semicolon after if
summary: A stray semicolon can make an if statement do nothing, while the code below it runs every time.
objectives: Explain what Java treats as the body of an if statement.
Trace what happens when a semicolon follows an if condition.
Recognize how indentation can hide the bug.
Fix the mistake with braces and check the program's behavior.

blocks.text: A semicolon ends a statement in Java. That is why this tiny mark can change what an `if` does. In this example, the writer wants the message to appear only when `temperature` is above 30.

bad.title: The semicolon ends the if body

good.title: The block is the if body

blocks.note: Both programs compile. The bad version also runs without a warning, but its condition does not control the message. The semicolon is the entire body of the `if`. The following block is separate, so it runs whether the condition is true or false.

blocks.text: An `if` controls the next statement. A statement can be a single line, a block inside braces, or even an empty statement made by a semicolon. In the bad example, Java sees the semicolon as the statement to control. The braces come after that statement, so they do not belong to the `if`.

blocks.caption: What Java does with if temperature > 30; followed by a block
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B{temperature > 30?}
  B -- yes --> C[Empty statement]
  B -- no --> D[Skip empty statement]
  C --> E[Run following block]
  D --> E
  E --> F([End])

blocks.text: The block runs on both paths. Indentation does not change this: Java follows the semicolon and matching braces, not how the code looks on the page.

blocks.title: Follow the statement
blocks.text: After an `if` condition, ask: what is the very next statement? If it is a stray `;`, the `if` controls only an empty statement.

sections.title: Trace it one step at a time

blocks.text: Let `temperature` be 20. Trace the bad version from top to bottom. Notice that the condition decides whether the empty statement runs, but the block comes afterward.

blocks.caption: Tracing if (temperature > 30); followed by a block

blocks.text: The message prints even though the condition is false. Without the semicolon, the block itself is the `if` body, so a false condition skips the block.
In each example, first decide what the condition should control. Then check whether the next statement is the intended one or a semicolon.

bad.title: A welcome prints for every visitor

good.title: Only a member gets the message

blocks.note: The condition is false because `isMember` is `false`. In the bad version, the semicolon is the `if` body and the message block runs afterward. Removing the semicolon puts the block under the condition.

bad.title: The number prints even when it is not positive

good.title: The message prints only for a positive number

blocks.note: Since `-2 > 0` is false, the fixed version skips the block. The bad version still reaches its separate block and prints the message.

blocks.text: The same stray semicolon can follow a `for` header. It makes the loop repeat an empty statement, then the block after the loop runs once. Another related trap is leaving out braces: only the first statement belongs to the `if`, even if indentation makes a second line look included.

good.title: The block is the loop body

blocks.note: In the bad version, the loop repeats an empty statement three times. The block after it runs once, so it prints `Hello` once, not three times.

bad.title: Indentation makes the second line look conditional

blocks.note: Without braces, only the first print statement belongs to the `if`. The second statement runs regardless of `score`. Java uses braces and statement structure, not indentation, to decide what is inside the `if`.

blocks.title: Make the structure visible
blocks.text: Use braces for every `if` body, even when it contains only one statement. Then a later change is less likely to leave a line outside the condition by accident.

blocks.question: What does this program print?
options: It prints Done only when count is above 0
blocks.explanation: The semicolon is the complete body of the `if`. The block after it is separate, so it runs and prints `Done`. This code compiles.

blocks.question: Which version prints `Ready` only when `isReady` is true?
blocks.explanation: In the second version, the block is the statement controlled by the `if`. The semicolon in the other versions ends the `if` body early.

blocks.question: How many times does `Hello` print?
blocks.explanation: The semicolon makes the loop body empty. The block after the loop runs once, after the loop finishes, so it prints `Hello` once.

items: Java compiles `if (condition);` as an `if` with an empty body. The semicolon is legal, so this mistake usually compiles without a warning.
A block after that semicolon is separate and runs regardless of the condition.
Java uses statements and matching braces to decide structure. Indentation does not control execution.
Use braces around the statements that should depend on an `if`.
When code runs unexpectedly, trace the statement immediately after the condition and check for a stray `;`.
